title: Walter Bishop, Jimmy Bertrand and percussion in Chicago
summary: Jones praises Walter Bishop and Jimmy Bertrand, who taught symphony players vibes, chimes and tympani, and again names Manzie Campbell.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: ...I'm sure in your travels you must have come in contact with Wally Bishop?

Of course, I mean, who else but Wally Bishop, until he had the accident with Earl Hines' band. I remember when Wally Bishop came through with Earl Hines. They had the Mills Brothers and they had the Palmer Brothers and they came through Kansas City. But also you must remember I knew Bishop before then. Then when they had that terrible accident that Cecil Irwin lost his life, through Iowa.
That's right. You had Walter Fuller but you had George Dixon, you see.
We just lost a great bass player, Hayes Alvis, just here recently this year.

What people don't know, that when Bishop lost the use of his legs, you see, he was mobile. But what they don't know that Bishop was not a drummer. He was a musician, not a percussionist; because Bishop was teaching peoples that you heard about that played in the Milwaukee Symphony. You heard of people that played in the Chicago Symphony. Walter Bishop was teaching these people

how to play the vibraphone chimes and tympts. But you must remember, Milt, before that advent there was nobody in the Chicago area that played like Jimmy Bertrand, you see, because to take those 4 tympanis and play - with

He played with Erskine Tate; he played with Carroll Dickerson. It's impossible for anybody to take the tympanis the way they were and set up and play "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles". That's when Red Nichols and other peoples were playing - Red Nichols was keeping his little jazz alive and they had this drummer, talking about how great he was, but they had to come from across the tracks to learn from him -
He was one of the first really versatile drummers. He played drums, xylophone -

That's the reason they started to call them guys percussionists, but now you must remember, the greatest drummer that ever lived was out in Chicago, that played with the Silas Green Show. His name was Manzie Campbell, But by Mancy being out of Chicago but being on the road on tour down South, nobody got a chance to see him. But out of that you got Jimmy Bertrand. Out of that you got Mr. Walter Bishop; and Walter taught the guys that played in Milwaukee Symphony, the guys that played in the Chicago

Symphony, the guys - Knapp /has a great big school out there and his son is carrying it on. But they had to come to Walter Bishop to learn how to play these vibraphone, chimes, glockenspiels and what have you.
